title: SYSK Selects: How The Human Microbiome Project Works
summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode, a rerun of the May 2014 episode on the Human Microbiome Project. The hosts explain the microbiome (gut bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi), how most cells in the body are microbial, and why a baseline healthy microbiome has been hard to define. They cover metagenomics as the key method that made the project possible, the project's volunteer recruitment and sampling of 18 body sites, its scale and data volume, and early findings: links to periodontal disease, probiotics, obesity, infant gut colonization at birth, immune system training and the hygiene hypothesis, allergies, and cancer. The episode closes with a listener email from a creationist biologist about natural selection and a sign-off.
rerun_of: How the Human Microbiome Project Works
topics: National Institutes of Health microbiome project

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, a May 2014 episode on the Human Microbiome Project, and Chuck joins for lighthearted banter. They lead into how gut health affects mood and serotonin.

segments.title: Microbes, archaea, and the tree of life
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the three domains of life (bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes), the discovery of archaea in the 1970s, and how archaea differ from bacteria. They recall the fecal transplant episode and C. difficile.

segments.title: How much of the body is microbial
segments.summary: The hosts describe the microbial share of the body: microbial genes outnumber human genes, microbes make up a small share of cells, bacterial body weight is a few pounds, and the mouth hosts many species. They also cover the virome acting as a predator on bacteria and the content of stool.

segments.title: Why the project was started and metagenomics
segments.summary: The NIH launched the project to map the human microbiome, aiming to find a healthy baseline. The hosts explain that metagenomics made this possible by sampling and sequencing microbes directly, rather than culturing them in the lab.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before the hosts return to the project.

segments.title: Volunteer recruitment, sampling, and project scale
segments.summary: The project recruited healthy volunteers, many of whom were rejected, and the accepted participants were treated for dental issues first. Sampling covered many body sites, over eleven thousand swabs were used, and the project cost about $170 million with about eighty institutions. Skin sites, the mouth, and the armpit are discussed, along with the 3.5 trillion bytes of data. The hosts also note that the sample group was narrow.

segments.title: Sponsor break and crawfish tangent
segments.summary: After a break, Josh and Chuck discuss crawfish boils and a family dish called garbage pail stew before returning to the findings.

segments.title: Early findings: gum disease, probiotics, and obesity
segments.summary: The hosts describe findings linking gum disease and cavity bacteria, the balance of microbes rather than eliminating them, the uncertain value of probiotics, and research where gut microbes from obese mice caused skinny mice to gain weight.

segments.title: Infant microbes, immune system, and allergies
segments.summary: Babies pick up bacteria from the birth canal that help them digest breast milk. The microbiome helps train the immune system, germ-free mice showed inflammation and bowel disease, and this ties to the hygiene hypothesis and allergies.

segments.title: Personalized medicine, cancer, and future episodes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the individuality of microbiomes, the idea of hyper-personalized medicine, a claim that some cancers hide from the immune system using bacteria, and a plan to revisit the microbiome in a future episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: creationist biologist
segments.summary: Josh reads an email from Eric in South Bend, Indiana, a Christian biologist who accepts microevolution and natural selection but not common descent, and says the two views share more common ground than differences.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and mention social media and email contact for the show.
